# Results: scheduled travel-time analytics for BMTC (PySpark)

*Generated by `src/make_docs.py`. Every number comes from files in `outputs/`. This analysis uses a **static, scraped timetable**: all times are
**scheduled (timetable-implied)**; no actual arrival times exist for Bengaluru, so sections 1-7 measure neither delay nor real congestion.
Section 8 adds a REAL actual-vs-scheduled delay analysis on a public Boston dataset to show the same Spark method on data that does contain actual times.*

## 2. Q1: scheduled variability and peak slowdown
Ranking requires at least 10 trips per segment and period (peak = 07-10h and 17-20h by hop start; the rest is off-peak).

- Segments (route, direction, from stop, to stop): 234,953 in total, **16,709** with enough peak trips to rank, 16,042 with enough in both periods.
- Among ranked segments, **89.6%** have exactly zero peak std dev (every trip has the same scheduled hop time). Median peak CV = 0.0000, 90th percentile 0.0000, maximum 0.691.
- Peak / off-peak mean hop-time ratio per segment: median 1.0000; 98.4% of ranked segments are within 1% of 1.0; 95th percentile 1.001; maximum 1.191.
- Pooled across routes (stop pairs): 6,825 ranked; median peak CV 0.0088, 90th percentile 0.0934; median slowdown 1.0000, 95th percentile 1.012.
- Routes (trip duration, per direction): 571 of 7,359 have enough peak trips; median peak CV 0.0000, 90th percentile 0.001, maximum 0.622.
- Scheduled headway CV per route/direction/stop/hour: median 0.505, 90th percentile 0.881 over 90,618 groups (at least 5 gaps each).

**Finding.** Scheduled variability is very low almost everywhere: most segments have the same planned hop time on every trip and no planned peak slowdown (ratio about 1.0). The timetable (see DATA_CARD.md, interpolation profile) appears to assume near-constant speed. The ranked lists below are therefore driven by a small number of unusual segments, often with different stop patterns or rounding, and should not be read as congestion hotspots.
The few high values were not investigated individually; with only the minimum number of trips they may reflect mixed stop patterns or single odd trips rather than planned congestion.

## 3. Q2: feeder vs trunk (heuristic classes)
Feeder segments (n=892) have a median scheduled hop speed of 21.65 km/h and median CV 0.0000; trunk segments (n=4,455) 21.52 km/h and 0.0000.

| route_class | ranked_segments | median_peak_speed_kmh | median_peak_cv | p90_peak_cv | median_slowdown_ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| feeder | 892 | 21.65 | 0.0 | 0.0 | 1.0 |
| trunk | 4455 | 21.52 | 0.0 | 0.0052 | 1.0 |

Rule: feeder = `route_short_name` starts with `MF-`; trunk = non-feeder with median trip length of at least 30 km. Routes per class: other 3176, trunk 1009, feeder 123. Speeds use straight-line distance. Differences in scheduled speed mostly reflect the timetable's assumed speed and stop spacing, not observed traffic.

## 4. Q3: performance (machine: Apple M3, 8 logical cores = 4 performance + 4 efficiency, 16.0 GB RAM; Spark 3.5.3, openjdk version "17.0.21" 2026-10-20, Python 3.11.13)
Baseline: Spark `local[1]`. Each core count ran in its own process; 1 discarded warm-up and 5 timed runs; `shuffle.partitions`=8; adaptive execution off; no caching between runs. Stage times each include their Parquet read and write (needed to force execution). Speedup S_N = T1 / TN on median total time.

| cores | clean s | join s | window+agg s | total median s | min-max s | throughput rows/s | speedup S_N | efficiency | oversubscribed |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 10.11 | 3.15 | 38.51 | 51.98 | 51.40 - 52.86 | 38,466 | 1.00 | 1.00 | False |
| 2 | 6.85 | 2.33 | 29.77 | 39.16 | 37.95 - 40.94 | 51,057 | 1.33 | 0.66 | False |
| 4 | 3.79 | 1.53 | 21.17 | 26.54 | 24.35 - 30.98 | 75,342 | 1.96 | 0.49 | False |

Per-stage speedup: 1 cores: clean 1.00, join 1.00, window_agg 1.00; 2 cores: clean 1.48, join 1.35, window_agg 1.29; 4 cores: clean 2.66, join 2.05, window_agg 1.82.

### Broadcast vs shuffle join (stage 2 only, local[4])

| join variant | median s | min-max s | shuffle write bytes (median/run) | plan file |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| broadcast | 1.854 | 1.507 - 1.980 | 2,633,151 | outputs/explain_join_broadcast.txt |
| shuffle | 2.728 | 2.590 - 2.883 | 219,268,237 | outputs/explain_join_shuffle.txt |

Broadcast = `F.broadcast()` hint on the small dimension tables (trips, routes, stops, service list). Shuffle = no hint and `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold=-1`, giving sort-merge joins with `Exchange` nodes (see the saved plans). Adaptive query execution is off so Spark cannot silently switch strategy. Shuffle bytes come from the Spark event log; broadcast data movement is not counted as shuffle.

### Synthetic scale-up (synthetic replication, not real data)

| replication | synthetic rows | cores | window+agg s |
|---|---|---|---|
| x1 | 1,999,285 | 1 | 42.71 |
| x1 | 1,999,285 | 4 | 34.38 |
| x5 | 9,996,425 | 1 | 208.32 |
| x5 | 9,996,425 | 4 | 159.33 |
| x10 | 19,992,850 | 1 | 446.47 |
| x10 | 19,992,850 | 4 | 255.83 |

Cleaned, joined rows were copied k times with new trip_id and route_id. Only the window + aggregation stage was timed, with 1 timed run per point and no discarded warm-up, and an 8g driver heap. Treat as indicative only.

**Reading.** 1 cores: S=1.00 (efficiency 1.00), 2 cores: S=1.33 (efficiency 0.66), 4 cores: S=1.96 (efficiency 0.49). The dataset is only about 1,999,285 rows, so fixed costs (JVM start-up of tasks, scheduling, CSV parsing of a 130 MB file, Parquet I/O, driver-side `toPandas`) are a large share of the run time and speedup is sub-linear; this chip has 4 efficiency cores besides 4 performance cores, which may also lower efficiency at higher N (not isolated in these measurements). Window and aggregation dominate the run time; the join stage is short.

## 5. Aggregation correctness (T22)
PASS: 13,148 hops and 3,375 segment-period groups from 432 sampled trips matched pandas (max abs speed diff 7.1e-15 km/h, max abs mean/std diff 1.4e-14 s). Test: `tests/test_pandas_crosscheck.py`.

## 6. Comparison with the base paper
Base paper as cited in our proposal: N. L. Mnyone and N. U. Amin (2026), *Real-Time Data Processing in Smart Transportation Using Apache Spark*, Preprints, DOI 10.20944/preprints202603.1261.v1.
**The team must confirm every statement about the paper from the paper itself; this project did not read it.** According to the proposal, the paper used synthetic GPS/vehicle-sensor logs, Spark Core RDDs and basic Spark SQL, and studied ingestion bottlenecks and memory use on single-table feeds. Contrast of *methodology only* (no numeric comparison):

| Aspect | Base paper (as stated in our proposal) | This project |
|---|---|---|
| Data | synthetic GPS / sensor logs | real, multi-table relational GTFS (routes, trips, stop_times, stops, calendar) |
| Structure | single-table feeds | four-way joins with orphan checks and a completeness waterfall |
| API | RDDs, basic Spark SQL | DataFrames, `Window` functions (lag per trip, per route-stop) |
| Metrics | ingestion bottlenecks, memory | sequence-level metrics (hop time, speed, scheduled headway), correctness cross-check |
| Join/shuffle | not part of our summary | measured broadcast vs sort-merge join with plans and shuffle bytes |

## 7. Limitations
1. **Scraped timetable.** Data come from the unofficial Namma BMTC 2.0 app scrape, which its maintainer calls unreliable; routes without live tracking are absent.
2. **Interpolated, near-constant-speed times** (DATA_CARD.md): little genuine variability is available to measure.
3. **No actual-time data.** Scheduled slowdown is a timetable-implied proxy for planned congestion, not a measure of it; no delay can be computed.
4. **Straight-line distance** underestimates road distance, so hop speeds are lower bounds.
5. **Small data versus Spark overhead:** about 1,999,285 rows; speedup is limited, and 1/2/4-core runs on a laptop with mixed core types are noisy.
6. **Heuristic feeder/trunk rule** (name prefix plus length), not an official BMTC classification.
7. **Few trips per segment:** the median route direction has only a handful of weekday trips, so the 10-trip minimum keeps only the busiest segments (16,709 of 234,953).
8. Dwell time is always 0 (arrival equals departure in the source).
9. Synthetic scale-up numbers are replicated data, not real, and use a single timed run per point.
10. Hop time-of-day uses the departure hour of the previous stop; trips that cross bucket boundaries are assigned by hop start.
11. Real delay is available only for the Boston dataset (section 8), not for Bengaluru.

## 8. Real delay analysis (Boston MBTA bus data: actual vs scheduled)
**Why this section exists.** BMTC publishes only a static timetable, so BMTC delay cannot be measured (sections 1-7 are therefore *scheduled* analytics).
To show the same Spark approach on **real actual-vs-scheduled times**, we ran it on the public MBTA (Boston) bus dataset, which records both the scheduled
and the actual departure of every bus at every timepoint. **Everything in this section is about Boston, not Bengaluru, and must not be quoted as BMTC performance.**
Source and licence: see `DATA_CARD_DELAY.md` (licence on the item: CC0). Months analysed: [1, 4, 7, 10] of 2024 (one per season).

### 8.1 Data completeness
9,108,352 raw events -> **4,606,471** kept (50.57%). Biggest steps: events with no actual time were dropped (data-collection gaps), and only 'Schedule'-standard trips
are judged on delay (the dataset says 'Headway'-standard trips must be judged on headways instead). Full waterfall: `outputs/tables/delay_waterfall.csv`.

| stage | rows_in | rows_out | pct_retained |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. raw arrival/departure rows | 9108352 | 9108352 | 100.0 |
| 2. drop null service_date/route/trip/order | 9108352 | 9108169 | 99.998 |
| 3. drop duplicate (date, trip, timepoint order) | 9108169 | 9108137 | 99.9996 |
| 4. drop rows without a valid scheduled time | 9108137 | 9108137 | 100.0 |
| 5. drop rows without an actual time | 9108137 | 8425094 | 92.5007 |
| 6. drop |delay| > 7200 s | 8425094 | 8424946 | 99.9982 |
| 7. keep schedule-standard trips | 8424946 | 4606471 | 54.6766 |

### 8.2 How late are buses?
Delay = actual minus scheduled departure at a timepoint. Over 4,606,471 events: mean **4.3 min**, median 3.0 min, 90th percentile 11.7 min.
**On time** (between -1 and +5 min) = **55.4%**; late (> 5 min) 34.1%; early 10.6%.

- By hour, the lowest on-time share is at 22h (48.4%) and the highest at 5h (67.6%). Overnight hours have fewer trips.
- Weekday mean delay: peak 4.4 min vs off-peak 4.2 min; weekend: peak 4.4 vs off-peak 4.7 min (peak = 07-10h and 17-20h scheduled hour).
- Delay by position in the trip (first 15 timepoints): 2.5 min at timepoint 1, a maximum of 5.0 min at timepoint 6, then 1.2 min at timepoint 14. The pattern is not monotonic, and later timepoints cover far fewer trips (a few thousand events at timepoint 14 vs hundreds of thousands at timepoint 1), so it is not a pure "delay accumulates" curve. By point type: start 2.5 min, middle 4.9 min, end 3.2 min.

Five most delayed routes (at least 100 events; `delay_by_route.csv`):

| route_id | n | mean_delay_sec | p90_delay_sec | on_time_rate |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 29 | 32612 | 510.96 | 1246 | 0.37 |
| CT2 | 46063 | 465.1 | 1037 | 0.37 |
| 47 | 69118 | 448.81 | 1113 | 0.42 |
| 245 | 6611 | 446.38 | 949 | 0.38 |
| 556 | 3774 | 402.13 | 945 | 0.47 |

### 8.3 Actual vs scheduled run time (real slowdown)
Between consecutive timepoints the mean scheduled run time is 315 s and the mean actual run time 323 s (on average 8.8 s added per hop; 3,882,783 hops).
Over 1,442 segments with enough peak and off-peak events, the median **actual** peak/off-peak slowdown ratio is **1.039** and the median **scheduled** ratio 1.036
(correlation between the two across segments: 0.39). Only 12.7% of Boston segments have a scheduled ratio within 1% of 1.0.

**Contrast with Bengaluru (method only).** In the BMTC timetable the median scheduled ratio is 1.000 and 98.4% of segments are within 1% of 1.0, i.e. a near-flat timetable.
The Boston timetable, in contrast, plans a different run time at peak for many segments. This shows that the BMTC finding "no scheduled slowdown" reflects how that feed was built, and why real delay needs actual-time data.
It does **not** say anything about how late BMTC buses really are.

### 8.4 Headway (bunching) on high-frequency routes
On 3,515,157 headway-standard events the mean ratio of actual to scheduled gap is 1.014; **17.2%** of gaps are under half the scheduled gap (bunching) and **14.6%** are over 1.5x (large gaps).

### 8.5 Performance on this real dataset
| cores | total median s | min-max s | throughput rows/s | speedup | efficiency |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 227.0 | 219.1 - 233.6 | 37,109 | 1.00 | 1.00 |
| 2 | 127.1 | 126.2 - 131.1 | 66,290 | 1.79 | 0.89 |
| 4 | 88.6 | 85.8 - 96.2 | 95,132 | 2.56 | 0.64 |

8,424,946 cleaned events; 3 timed runs after 1 discarded warm-up per core count; each core count in its own process; stages = ingest+clean and window+aggregation; 6g driver heap. This is real data (no replication), so it shows how speedup behaves at a more realistic volume than the Bengaluru timetable.

### 8.6 Correctness
PASS: 14,458 events on 6 routes recomputed in pandas directly from the raw CSV matched Spark (max abs diff in mean/std/on-time 6.8e-13). Tests: `tests/test_delay.py`.

### 8.7 Limitations of the delay part
1. Boston, not Bengaluru: different operator, city, fleet and timetable practice.
2. Only timepoints (not every stop) and only departures are recorded; delay is departure delay at timepoints.
3. 'Actual' times come from MBTA's own vehicle tracking; the dataset notes data is not guaranteed complete for any stop or date, and 7.5% of events had no actual time.
4. Four sampled months (one per season) of 2024, not the full year; no claim about other months.
5. 'Headway'-standard trips are not judged on schedule delay, so delay figures cover only 'Schedule'-standard trips.
6. Peak is defined by scheduled hour (07-10h and 17-20h), the same windows as the Bengaluru analysis.
